title: Picard Proximal Monte Carlo for Parallel Bayesian Imaging with Score-Based Generative Priors

paper.title: Picard Proximal Monte Carlo for Parallel Bayesian Imaging with Score-Based Generative Priors
paper.abstract: Abstract Bayesian imaging inverse problems often require sampling from high-dimensional posterior distributions. While recent score-based and diffusion models provide expressive Bayesian priors, their sampling procedures remain inherently sequential and computationally expensive for large-scale imaging applications. We propose PiX-MC , a time-parallel posterior sampling framework based on proximal Langevin dynamics and Picard iteration. The proximal-likelihood formulation exploits the fact that many imaging likelihoods admit efficient, problem-specific proximal operators, while Picard refinement exposes parallelism across discretization nodes and naturally supports multi-GPU implementation. To further improve practical scalability and sampling performance, we develop multi-block and annealed variants of the proposed framework. We establish convergence guarantees under transparent assumptions, accommodating non-log-concave posteriors, imperfect learned score models, multi-block implementations, and annealing schedules. Experiments on a diverse collection of imaging inverse problems demonstrate that PiX-MC substantially reduces wall-clock time while preserving reconstruction quality. On a 512 × 512 × 80 512\times 512\times 80 sparse-view computed tomography (CT) problem, annealed multi-block PiX-MC achieves up to a 50 × 50\times runtime speedup over the standard Langevin sampler using eight GPUs.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The recovery of an unknown image 𝒙 ∈ ℝ d {\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from a set of sparse and noisy measurements 𝒚 ∈ ℝ c {\bm{y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c} is a fundamental problem in computational imaging. It is often mathematically formulated as an inverse problem of the following system 𝒚 = 𝑨 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) + 𝒆 , {\bm{y}}={\bm{A}}({\bm{x}})+{\bm{e}}, (1) where the forward operator 𝑨 : ℝ d → ℝ c {\bm{A}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{c} models the imaging system response and 𝒆 ∈ ℝ c {\bm{e}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c} denotes measurement noise. Due to the sparsity and noisiness of 𝒚 {\bm{y}} , multiple plausible 𝒙 {\bm{x}} can explain the same set of measurements, leading to significant uncertainty in the recovered image. Bayesian sampling methods offer a principled framework for addressing this ambiguity. Rather than seeking a single point estimate, they aim to characterize the full posterior distribution π ⁡ ( 𝒙 | 𝒚 ) \pi({\bm{x}}|{\bm{y}}) given an image prior p ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) p({\bm{x}}) . This capability is particularly beneficial in high-stakes biomedical and scientific imaging applications, where different imaging results can lead to different scientific conclusions, clinical decisions, or downstream actions ( Begoli et al., 2019 ; Kampourakis and McCain, 2019 ) . Traditionally, the image prior is handcrafted, including total variation and sparsity-promoting penalties ( Rudin et al., 1992 ; Sauer and Bouman, 1992 ; Gu et al., 2014 ) ; yet such priors often fall short in capturing the complexity of real-world image distributions. Recently, score-based diffusion models (SDMs) have emerged as a powerful class of generative models capable of modeling such complexity, inspiring a growing body of work on SDM-based posterior sampling for imaging inverse problems. One popular line of work incorporates measurements as guidance to steer the generative process toward the posterior distribution ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Chung et al., 2022 ) ; this approach is convenient to implement on top of pre-trained models and has been demonstrated across a wide range of imaging applications ( Chung and Ye, 2022 ; Song et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ) . However, such guidance-based methods generally lack theoretical guarantees on whether the generated samples indeed follow the true posterior, significantly limiting their interpretability and reliability in high-stakes settings. In light of this, another class of methods integrates SDMs with classical Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) frameworks, providing more rigorous posterior sampling guarantees ( Brooks et al., 2011 ) . Popular instantiations include combining Langevin dynamics with the score network of an SDM ( Jalal et al., 2021 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , and incorporating a full SDM as an empirical proximal sampler in the split Gibbs process ( Coeurdoux et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Despite their algorithmic differences, these methods share a common sequential structure: samples must be evolved through long iterative trajectories, each requiring repeated evaluations of both the score model and the forward operator. As a result, the computational cost scales poorly with the problem dimension and the complexity of the forward model, making large-scale imaging applications particularly challenging. This limitation is increasingly pronounced as modern machine learning systems are routinely deployed on multiple graphics processing unit (multi-GPU) platforms that offer substantial Figure 1 : Schematic illustration of the proposed Picard Proximal Monte Carlo (PiX-MC) method. PiX-MC employs time-batch processing and exploits Picard iteration to enable parallel computation across time nodes. parallel computational resources; yet existing samplers are not designed to exploit such parallelism. While efforts have explored parallelism for solvers applicable to inverse problems ( Lian et al., 2015 ; Zhou et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2021 ) , they are largely restricted to deterministic optimization frameworks, limiting the direct applicability of these techniques to posterior sampling. In this work, we bridge this gap by proposing Pi card pro X imal M onte C arlo ( PiX-MC ) , a time-parallel posterior sampling framework for scalable Bayesian imaging. PiX-MC is built upon a forward-backward splitting of Langevin dynamics that decouples the prior and likelihood, enabling modular integration of a score-based generative prior and a likelihood update via proximal mapping . To overcome the sequential bottleneck, PiX-MC further leverages Picard iteration to parallelize the sampling trajectory across time steps. A schematic illustration is provided in Figure 1 . The key contributions of this work are as follows: • We formulate the sampling trajectory of PiX-MC as a fixed-point problem and solve it via Picard iteration. Rather than parallelizing across image pixels, PiX-MC introduces parallelism across time steps, enabling concurrent processing over multiple GPUs. Unlike existing Picard-based methods ( Shih et al., 2023 ; Anari et al., 2024 ) , PiX-MC incorporates a forward–backward formulation that imposes measurement consistency through a proximal update. This design is particularly attractive for computational imaging, as it naturally exploits the structure of many imaging forward operators. We further develop annealed and multi-block variants of PiX-MC. The former employs temperature annealing to accelerate the underlying sequential sampling trajectory, while the latter partitions the sampling trajectory into multiple blocks, allowing PiX-MC to still operate efficiently under limited GPU budgets. • We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the proposed suite of PiX-MC algorithms. Our analysis bounds the time-averaged relative Fisher information by an O ⁡ ( 1 / T ) O(1/T) transient term together with explicit approximation-error terms. The theory accommodates imperfect learned score networks and weakly convex imaging likelihoods, covering practical settings encountered in a wide range of imaging problems. Furthermore, our results provide a detailed error decomposition that explicitly characterizes the individual contributions of forward–backward splitting, Picard iterations, and time discretization, offering interpretable insight into the sources of sampling error. • We validate PiX-MC on a diverse set of computational imaging inverse problems, including both linear and nonlinear forward models. In addition, we consider large-scale problems ranging from 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 image deblurring to 512 × 512 × 80 512\times 512\times 80 sparse-view computed tomography (CT), covering both 2D and 3D imaging settings. These experiments are conducted on multi-GPU platforms to reflect realistic deployment conditions. The results demonstrate that PiX-MC generalizes across these settings while substantially reducing wall-clock time without sacrificing reconstruction quality. On the large-scale 3D CT task, APiX-MC achieves up to a 50 × 50\times runtime speedup over the standard Langevin sampler using eight GPUs.

sections.heading: 2 Background and Related Works
sections.text: We begin by reviewing regularized image reconstruction from a Bayesian perspective. We then introduce SDMs and discuss posterior sampling methods for imaging inverse problems. Finally, we review related parallelization approaches for image reconstruction.

sections.heading: 2.1 Bayesian Image Reconstruction
sections.text: Classical approaches to imaging inverse problems are formulated as regularized optimization problems, seeking a solution that simultaneously fits the measurements and conforms to prior knowledge about the image. This strong generative capability makes score-based diffusion models particularly attractive as image priors for solving inverse problems, as discussed in the next section.

sections.heading: 2.3 Posterior Sampling Methods for Imaging
sections.text: Existing posterior sampling methods can largely be viewed as constructing stochastic processes whose stationary or terminal distribution approximates the target posterior π ⁡ ( 𝒙 | 𝒚 ) \pi({\bm{x}}|{\bm{y}}) . These methods can be roughly categorized into three families according to the type of their stochastic process: Langevin-based methods, split Gibbs samplers, and reverse-time diffusion approaches.

sections.heading: Split Gibbs Samplers
sections.text: An alternative approach to posterior sampling is based on variable splitting and Gibbs sampling ( Vono et al., 2019 ; Pereyra et al., 2023 ; Bouman and Buzzard, 2023 ; Faye et al., 2024 ) . These methods introduce an auxiliary variable 𝒛 {\bm{z}} and couple it with 𝒙 {\bm{x}} through a quadratic penalty 1 2 ​ ρ ​ ‖ 𝒙 − 𝒛 ‖ 2 \frac{1}{2\rho}\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{z}}\|^{2} , where ρ > 0 \rho>0 controls the coupling strength. Sampling is then performed by alternating between the conditional distributions 𝒙 n + 1 \displaystyle{{\bm{x}}_{n+1}} ∼ 𝖾𝗑𝗉 ⁡ ( − L ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) − 1 2 ​ ρ ​ ‖ 𝒙 − 𝒛 n ‖ 2 ) \displaystyle\sim\mathsf{exp}\left(-L({\bm{x}})-\frac{1}{2\rho}\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{z}}_{n}\|^{2}\right) (12a) 𝒛 n + 1 \displaystyle{{\bm{z}}_{n+1}} ∼ 𝖾𝗑𝗉 ⁡ ( − V ⁡ ( 𝒛 ) − 1 2 ​ ρ ​ ‖ 𝒛 − 𝒙 n + 1 ‖ 2 ) . \displaystyle\sim\mathsf{exp}\left(-V({\bm{z}})-\frac{1}{2\rho}\|{\bm{z}}-{\bm{x}}_{n+1}\|^{2}\right). (12b) The resulting decoupling allows the likelihood and prior terms to be handled independently, making it possible to exploit the structure of the forward model while incorporating sophisticated learned priors in a modular fashion. Recent works have employed diffusion models to approximate the prior conditional distribution in ( 12b ), establishing convergence to the augmented posterior under various conditions ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Coeurdoux et al., 2024b ; Xu and Chi, 2024 ) , with extensions to blind inverse problem settings ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Despite these advances, the conditional updates remain computationally demanding, as each Gibbs iteration typically requires solving an additional sampling subproblem.

sections.heading: Guided Reverse Diffusion
sections.text: Rather than constructing a Markov chain that directly targets the posterior distribution, guided reverse-diffusion methods modify the reverse diffusion trajectory using measurement information. Starting from a learned generative diffusion process, the reverse dynamics are guided toward measurement-consistent samples through likelihood-based corrections ( Chung et al., 2022 ) or approximations of the posterior score ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . This viewpoint underlies a broad class of diffusion posterior sampling and guided diffusion methods, which have demonstrated strong empirical performance across a wide range of imaging tasks ( Chung and Ye, 2022 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Kawar et al., 2022 ; Rout et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Compared with Langevin-based approaches, however, these methods typically rely on approximations of the time-dependent posterior score and therefore do not always admit a straightforward characterization in terms of a target invariant distribution.

sections.heading: 2.4 Related Parallel Imaging Methods & Picard Iteration
sections.text: Most existing parallel methods consider a general optimization formulation applicable to the MAP problem in ( 2 ). They accelerate computation by exploiting parallelism within individual iterations, including stochastic gradient methods ( Recht et al., 2011 ; Lian et al., 2017 ) , block-coordinate updates ( Fercoq and Richtárik, 2015 ; Richtárik and Takáč, 2016 ) , and asynchronous procedures ( Peng et al., 2016 ; Sun et al., 2017 ; Hannah et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2021 ) . Some of these techniques have also been extended to sampling ( Salim et al., 2019 ; Salim and Richtarik, 2020 ; Ding et al., 2021 ) . However, they do not reduce the intrinsic sequential structure of iterative algorithms, which remains the fundamental computational bottleneck for large-scale posterior sampling. A more recent line of work seeks to parallelize the sampling trajectory itself. In image generation, Picard iteration has been used to evaluate multiple denoising steps simultaneously ( Shih et al., 2023 ; So et al., 2025 ) . Consider a dynamical system d ​ 𝒙 t = f t ​ ( 𝒙 t ) ​ d ​ t d{\bm{x}}_{t}=f_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})\,dt , t ∈ [ 0 , T ] t\in[0,T] , with initial condition 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} . Picard iteration generates a sequence of trajectories according to 𝒙 t ( 0 ) ≡ 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 t ( k + 1 ) = 𝒙 0 + ∫ 0 t f s ( 𝒙 s ( k ) ) d s , for k = 0 , … , K − 1 . {\bm{x}}_{t}^{(0)}\equiv{\bm{x}}_{0},\quad{\bm{x}}_{t}^{(k+1)}={\bm{x}}_{0}+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}f_{s}({\bm{x}}_{s}^{(k)})\,ds,\quad\text{for }k=0,\ldots,K-1. (13) Note that each point 𝒙 t ( k + 1 ) {\bm{x}}_{t}^{(k+1)} depends only on the previous trajectory ( 𝒙 s ( k ) ) s ∈ [ 0 , t ] ({\bm{x}}_{s}^{(k)})_{s\in[0,t]} , rather than on 𝒙 s ( k + 1 ) {\bm{x}}_{s}^{(k+1)} for s < t s<t . This formulation breaks the sequential dependency across time and allows 𝒙 t ( k + 1 ) {\bm{x}}_{t}^{(k+1)} to be computed in parallel across time nodes after discretization. On the theoretical side, Anari et al. (2024) established parallelization guarantees for Langevin dynamics under functional inequalities such as logarithmic Sobolev, with subsequent works extending these ideas to diffusion models ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , diagonal trajectory updates ( Zhou and Sugiyama, 2025 ) , and higher-order Langevin schemes ( Mahajan et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, existing trajectory-parallel methods are designed primarily for either unconditional generative models or posterior distributions with explicit unnormalized densities. They do not directly accommodate the structure of Bayesian imaging posteriors, which often combine proximal likelihood updates, learned image priors, and annealing schedules. PiX-MC significantly extends this line of work to posterior sampling for imaging inverse problems, and provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis that accommodates all these components.

sections.heading: 3 Method: Picard Proximal Monte Carlo (PiX-MC)
sections.text: This section presents the proposed PiX-MC framework. We first construct a proximal-likelihood drift motivated by the FBS-style update, which induces a sequential proximal Langevin dynamics. We then reformulate the resulting dynamics using Picard iteration, enabling parallel computation across sequential time steps. We further establish finite-horizon bounds on the time-averaged relative Fisher information of PiX-MC under transparent assumptions. Finally, we introduce multi-block and annealed variants of PiX-MC to further improve scalability and imaging performance. The analysis extends to both variants under their stated variant-specific assumptions.

Our presentation follows a two-part structure: we first introduce the formulation of each algorithm, and then establish its companion convergence analysis, with additional assumptions and lemmas introduced as needed. sections.text: We apply Picard iteration to parallelize the computation of the X-MC trajectory across time nodes. Let t n = n ​ γ t_{n}=n\gamma for n = 0 , … , N n=0,\ldots,N , where N ​ γ = T N\gamma=T . Discretizing ( 24 ) using left-point Riemann sums yields the PiX-MC update 𝒙 n ( 0 ) = 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 0 ( k ) = 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 n ( k + 1 ) = 𝒙 0 − γ ​ ∑ i = 0 n − 1 T η ​ ( 𝒙 i ( k ) ) + 2 ​ 𝑩 n ​ γ \displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{n}^{(0)}={\bm{x}}_{0},\quad{\bm{x}}_{0}^{(k)}={\bm{x}}_{0},\quad{\bm{x}}_{n}^{(k+1)}={\bm{x}}_{0}-\gamma\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathsfit{T}_{\eta}({\bm{x}}_{i}^{(k)})+\sqrt{2}{\bm{B}}_{n\gamma} (25) with n = 1 , … , N , k = 0 , … , K . \displaystyle\text{with}\quad n=1,\ldots,N,\quad k=0,\ldots,K. Here, 𝑩 n ​ γ = ∑ i = 1 n γ ​ 𝑾 i {\bm{B}}_{n\gamma}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{\gamma}{\bm{W}}_{i} denotes the cumulative sum of the discrete Brownian increments. Unlike the sequential update rule of X-MC, PiX-MC has the entire previous trajectory { 𝒙 n ( k ) } n = 0 N \{{\bm{x}}_{n}^{(k)}\}_{n=0}^{N} available when computing { 𝒙 n ( k + 1 ) } n = 0 N \{{\bm{x}}_{n}^{(k+1)}\}_{n=0}^{N} . Hence, the drift evaluations T η ​ ( 𝒙 0 ( k ) ) , … , T η ​ ( 𝒙 N − 1 ( k ) ) \mathsfit{T}_{\eta}({\bm{x}}_{0}^{(k)}),\ldots,\\ \mathsfit{T}_{\eta}({\bm{x}}_{N-1}^{(k)}) can be computed in parallel across time nodes and accumulated for the next trajectory refinement. Suppose sufficient parallel computational resources are available such that each time node can be processed concurrently; the computational cost of PiX-MC then no longer scales with N N but with the number of Picard iterations K K . This is equivalent to viewing the entire trajectory as a single time block that is fully parallelized. Algorithm 1 summarizes the algorithmic details of PiX-MC under this single-block condition. In § 3.3 , we will introduce a multi-block version that better balances computational resource constraints against the degree of parallelization.

sections.text: The goal of the presented analysis is to quantify the distance between the evolving probability distribution of the PiX-MC iterates 𝒙 n ( k ) {\bm{x}}_{n}^{(k)} and the target posterior distribution. To this end, we use the relative Fisher information to measure the distance between two probability distributions. Definition 1 . Let μ \mu and π \pi denote two probability distributions such that μ ≪ π \mu\ll\pi . The Fisher information (FI) of μ \mu relative to π \pi is defined as 𝖥𝖨 ( μ ∥ π ) = ∫ ‖ ∇ 𝗅𝗈𝗀 d ​ μ d ​ π ‖ 2 d μ . \mathsf{FI}(\mu\|\pi)=\int\left\|\nabla\mathsf{log\,}\frac{d\mu}{d\pi}\right\|^{2}d\mu. From an optimization perspective, Langevin dynamics can be viewed as a gradient flow in the space of probability distributions equipped with the Wasserstein metric, with FI playing the role of the squared gradient norm. Thus, relative FI provides a stationarity criterion for the algorithm. Lemma 2 . Let μ 0 \mu_{0} be the initial distribution of 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} and suppose Assumptions 1 - 2 hold. As shown by the numerical results in Fig. 3 and § 5 , this geometric rate leads to rapid stabilization of the trajectories within only a few iterations. We next present the main theorem for PiX-MC. sections.heading: 3.3 Multi-Block PiX-MC: Partitioning the Trajectory into Multiple Blocks
sections.text: As discussed in the previous section, the vanilla PiX-MC treats the entire trajectory as a single block to be fully parallelized, offering the largest possible degree of parallelism. Yet this design comes with two practical trade-offs. First, the degree of parallelism interacts with the choice of hyperparameters. Recall from Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 that controlling the Picard error requires q 𝗌𝗂𝗇𝗀 < 1 q_{\mathsf{sing}}<1 . Since q 𝗌𝗂𝗇𝗀 = T ​ Λ η q_{\mathsf{sing}}=T\Lambda_{\eta} , this contraction condition directly restricts the time horizon that can be handled in a single block. Second, refining the full trajectory at once is more demanding on computational resources, as it requires storing and updating all time nodes simultaneously, which can be memory-intensive for large-scale imaging problems. To better balance parallelism with these practical considerations, we introduce multi-block PiX-MC that partitions the trajectory into multiple time blocks.

sections.heading: Algorithm formulation.
sections.text: We partition the full interval [ 0 , T ] [0,T] into M M successive blocks, each spanning N N time steps, so that T = M ​ N ​ γ , τ = N ​ γ , T=MN\gamma,\qquad\tau=N\gamma, (32) where τ \tau denotes the length of each block. Starting from the endpoint of the preceding block, multi-block PiX-MC then performs K K Picard refinements only within the current block, rather than over the full trajectory. As a result, both the trajectory storage and the concurrent drift evaluations scale with the block size N N rather than the total number of time steps M ​ N MN , allowing N N to be chosen according to the available GPU memory and parallel computing resources. This block-wise refinement also relaxes the condition required for convergence: the local Picard contraction factor becomes q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 ≜ τ ​ Λ η q_{\mathsf{mult}}\,\triangleq\,\tau\Lambda_{\eta} . Note that when M > 1 M>1 , q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 = ( τ / T ) ​ q 𝗌𝗂𝗇𝗀 < q 𝗌𝗂𝗇𝗀 q_{\mathsf{mult}}=(\tau/T)q_{\mathsf{sing}}<q_{\mathsf{sing}} , the multi-block scheme admits a larger stepsize than its single-block counterpart. Algorithm 2 summarizes the complete procedure of multi-block PiX-MC. As shown, parallelization occurs within each time block, while the algorithm proceeds sequentially across blocks. sections.heading: Convergence analysis.
sections.text: The convergence analysis of multi-block PiX-MC requires an additional stability control compared with the single-block setting. In single-block PiX-MC, every Picard trajectory is initialized at the same point 𝒙 0 {\bm{x}}_{0} , and the initial Picard residual can be controlled directly through the initial Fisher information. In contrast, the starting point 𝒙 m ​ N {\bm{x}}_{mN} of the m m -th block is itself a random variable, determined by the output of all preceding blocks. Therefore, we impose the following stability assumption on the block starting points, which allows the initial Picard residual to be controlled uniformly across blocks. Assumption 3 . The block starting points have uniformly bounded second moments. Specifically, there exists a constant C 𝒙 > 0 C_{\bm{x}}>0 , independent of the number of blocks M M and the total time horizon T T , such that 𝗌𝗎𝗉 0 ≤ m ≤ M − 1 𝔼 ​ ‖ 𝒙 m ​ N ( 0 ) ‖ 2 ≤ C 𝒙 . \mathop{\mathsf{sup}}\limits_{0\leq m\leq M-1}\mathbb{E}\left\|{\bm{x}}^{(0)}_{mN}\right\|^{2}\leq C_{\bm{x}}. (33) Assumption 3 is a standard condition for Langevin-based methods, and can be implied by coercivity of the posterior potential or dissipativity of the drift; see e.g., ( Raginsky et al., 2017 ; Renaud et al., 2026a ) . We also provide an example condition for Assumption 3 to hold in Appendix C . This assumption is consistent with practical imaging settings, where the image intensity typically lies in a bounded range such as [ 0 , 1 ] d [0,1]^{d} . Under Assumption 3 , the block-wise Picard initialization remains uniformly controlled over the sampling horizon. We next establish a result analogous to Lemma 2 for multi-block PiX-MC. Lemma 3 . Let Assumptions 1 – 3 hold, and set the parameters η , γ > 0 \eta,\gamma>0 sufficiently small such that 1 − η ​ α L > 0 , 1 − 3 ​ η 2 ​ β L 2 > 0 , q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 = γ ​ N ​ Λ η < 1 . 1-\eta\alpha_{L}>0,\quad 1-3\eta^{2}\beta_{L}^{2}>0,\quad q_{\mathsf{mult}}=\gamma N\Lambda_{\eta}<1. (34) For each block m = 0 , … , M − 1 m=0,\ldots,M-1 , define the in-block Picard error as ε m , k ≜ 𝗆𝖺𝗑 i = 1 , … , N 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝒙 m ​ N + i ( k ) − 𝒙 m ​ N + i ( k − 1 ) ‖ 2 ] . \varepsilon_{m,k}\,\triangleq\,\mathop{\mathsf{max}}_{i=1,\ldots,N}\mathbb{E}\left[\|{\bm{x}}_{mN+i}^{(k)}-{\bm{x}}_{mN+i}^{(k-1)}\|^{2}\right]. (35) Then, for multi-block PiX-MC, the in-block Picard error satisfies ε m , k + 1 ≤ q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 2 ​ ε m , k \varepsilon_{m,k+1}\leq q_{\mathsf{mult}}^{2}\,\varepsilon_{m,k} . Consequently, for each block m = 0 , … , M − 1 m=0,\ldots,M-1 , ε m , K ≤ q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 2 ​ K − 2 ​ [ 2 ​ τ ​ d + 3 ​ τ 2 ​ ( δ 2 + G 2 ) 1 − 3 ​ η 2 ​ β L 2 ] = q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 2 ​ K − 2 ​ R . \varepsilon_{m,K}\leq q_{\mathsf{mult}}^{2K-2}\left[2\tau d+\displaystyle\frac{3\tau^{2}(\delta^{2}+G^{2})}{1-3\eta^{2}\beta_{L}^{2}}\right]=q_{\mathsf{mult}}^{2K-2}R. (36) Here G > 0 G>0 is a constant independent of the total time T T ; see Appendix D for details. Proof. See Appendix D for the detailed proof and explicit expressions for the constants. ∎ Lemma 3 establishes geometric Picard contraction within each local block. We are now ready to present the convergence result for multi-block PiX-MC. Theorem 2 . Let ( μ t ) t ≥ 0 (\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0} denote the law of the continuous interpolation of { 𝒙 n ( K ) } n = 0 M ​ N \{{{\bm{x}}_{n}}^{(K)}\}_{n=0}^{MN} generated by multi-block PiX-MC, where N > 0 N>0 denotes the number of time steps in each time block and M > 0 M>0 is the number of blocks. Assume Assumptions 1 - 3 hold and choose sufficiently small parameters η , γ > 0 \eta,\gamma>0 . Then, the following inequality holds for multi-block PiX-MC: ( 0.75 − 𝒪 ( η 2 ) − 𝒪 ( γ 2 ) ) 1 T ∫ 0 T 𝖥𝖨 ( μ t ∥ π ) d t ≤ 𝖪𝖫 ( μ 0 ∥ π ) T + 𝒪 ⁡ ( η 2 ) ⏟ Splitting discrepancy + 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ 2 ) ⏟ Score mismatch error + 𝒪 ⁡ ( γ ) ⏟ Discretization error + 𝒪 ⁡ ( q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 2 ​ K − 2 ) ​ R ⏟ Finite Picard refinement error . \begin{array}[]{rl}&\Big(0.75-\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})-\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{2})\Big)\;\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathsf{FI}(\mu_{t}\|\pi)dt\\ \leq&\displaystyle\frac{\mathsf{KL}(\mu_{0}\|\pi)}{T}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Splitting}\\ \text{discrepancy}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2})}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Score mismatch}\\ \text{error}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(\gamma)}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Discretization}\\ \text{error}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(q_{\mathsf{mult}}^{2K-2})\,R}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Finite Picard}\\ \text{refinement error}\end{subarray}}.\end{array} (37) where R R is the constant from Lemma 3 . Proof. See Appendix D for the detailed proof and range of the hyperparameters. ∎ Theorem 2 extends the single-block guarantee to the multi-block case by replacing the global contraction coefficient with the in-block q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 < 1 q_{\mathsf{mult}}<1 . Note that q 𝗆𝗎𝗅𝗍 q_{\mathsf{mult}} is determined by the local time horizon τ \tau rather than the total sampling time T T , and the finite Picard error still decays geometrically within each block. Compared with the result in Theorem 1 , the associated constant is now controlled by R R established in Lemma 3 , rather than by the initial Fisher information.

sections.heading: 3.4 Multi-Block Annealed PiX-MC: Improving Sample Quality via Annealing
sections.text: PiX-MC has so far used a fixed noise level in the score network S θ {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta} . In this section, we introduce multi-block annealed PiX-MC ( multi-block APiX-MC ) that employs a decreasing noise schedule to first capture coarse image structures and then progressively refine details.

sections.heading: Algorithm formulation.
sections.text: Let n = m ​ N + i n=mN+i denote the global time node index, where m = 0 , … , M − 1 m=0,\ldots,M-1 is the block index and i = 0 , … , N − 1 i=0,\ldots,N-1 is the local node index. We use the geometric schedule σ n = 𝗆𝖺𝗑 { σ 𝗆𝖺𝗑 ​ ξ n , σ 𝗆𝗂𝗇 } , \sigma_{n}=\mathop{\mathsf{max}}\{\sigma_{\mathop{\mathsf{max}}}\xi^{n},\sigma_{\mathop{\mathsf{min}}}\}, (38) where 0 < ξ < 1 0<\xi<1 is the annealing parameter. We further associate { σ n } n = 0 M ​ N − 1 \{\sigma_{n}\}_{n=0}^{MN-1} with a non-increasing score-weight schedule { α n } n = 0 M ​ N − 1 \{\alpha_{n}\}_{n=0}^{MN-1} satisfying α n ≥ 1 \alpha_{n}\geq 1 and α n → 1 \alpha_{n}\to 1 when n → ∞ n\to\infty . (39) Rather than restarting the annealing schedule at each block boundary, the global indexing in ( 38 ) allows the noise level and score weight to decrease continuously over the entire sampling trajectory. sections.heading: Convergence analysis.
sections.text: The convergence analysis follows the same overall argument as that of multi-block PiX-MC, with modifications accounting for the time-varying denoising-strength schedule σ n \sigma_{n} and score-weight schedule α n \alpha_{n} . Since the proximal drift T η , σ α \mathsfit{T}_{\eta,\sigma}^{\alpha} now varies across time nodes, we replace the single score-mismatch error δ \delta with the node-dependent error and adjust the uniform Lipschitz bound of the proximal drift accordingly. To control these effects, we replace Assumption 2 with the following annealed counterpart. Assumption 4 . Given the schedules { σ n } n = 0 M ​ N − 1 \{\sigma_{n}\}_{n=0}^{MN-1} and { α n } n = 0 M ​ N − 1 \{\alpha_{n}\}_{n=0}^{MN-1} , there exist { δ n } n = 0 M ​ N − 1 \{\delta_{n}\}_{n=0}^{MN-1} , L S > 0 L_{\mathsfit{S}}>0 , and R S > 0 R_{\mathsfit{S}}>0 such that the score network S θ {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta} satisfies: (i) for every n = 0 , … , M ​ N − 1 n=0,\ldots,MN-1 and 𝒙 ∈ ℝ d {\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , ‖ S θ ​ ( 𝒙 , σ n ) − ∇ V ​ ( 𝒙 ) ‖ ≤ δ n ; \left\|{\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}\left({\bm{x}};\sigma_{n}\right)-\nabla V({\bm{x}})\right\|\leq\delta_{n}; (40) (ii) for every n = 0 , … , M ​ N − 1 n=0,\ldots,MN-1 and 𝒙 , 𝒛 ∈ ℝ d {\bm{x}},{\bm{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , ‖ S θ ​ ( 𝒙 , σ n ) − S θ ​ ( 𝒛 , σ n ) ‖ ≤ L S ​ ‖ 𝒙 − 𝒛 ‖ ; \left\|{\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}\left({\bm{x}};\sigma_{n}\right)-{\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}\left({\bm{z}};\sigma_{n}\right)\right\|\leq L_{\mathsfit{S}}\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{z}}\|; (41) (iii) for every n = 0 , … , M ​ N − 1 n=0,\ldots,MN-1 and 𝒙 ∈ ℝ d {\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , ‖ S θ ​ ( 𝒙 , σ n ) ‖ ≤ R S . \left\|{\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}\left({\bm{x}};\sigma_{n}\right)\right\|\leq R_{\mathsfit{S}}. (42) Assumption 4(iii) controls the additional discrepancy induced by the score weights. Indeed, ‖ α n ​ S θ ​ ( 𝒙 , σ n ) − ∇ V ​ ( 𝒙 ) ‖ ≤ δ n + ( α n − 1 ) ​ R S . \left\|\alpha_{n}{\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}\left({\bm{x}};\sigma_{n}\right)-\nabla V({\bm{x}})\right\|\leq\delta_{n}+\left(\alpha_{n}-1\right)R_{\mathsfit{S}}. (43) Accordingly, define the maximal and time-averaged annealed-score errors by δ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 ≜ 𝗆𝖺𝗑 0 ≤ n ≤ M ​ N − 1 { δ n + ( α n − 1 ) ​ R S } , δ ¯ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 2 ≜ 1 M ​ N ​ ∑ n = 0 M ​ N − 1 [ δ n + ( α n − 1 ) ​ R S ] 2 . \delta_{\mathsf{ann}}\,\triangleq\,\mathop{\mathsf{max}}\limits_{0\leq n\leq MN-1}\left\{\delta_{n}+\left(\alpha_{n}-1\right)R_{\mathsfit{S}}\right\},\quad\bar{\delta}_{\mathsf{ann}}^{2}\,\triangleq\,\frac{1}{MN}\sum\limits_{n=0}^{MN-1}\left[\delta_{n}+\left(\alpha_{n}-1\right)R_{\mathsfit{S}}\right]^{2}. (44) The maximal score error δ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 \delta_{\mathsf{ann}} controls the in-block Picard error, whereas δ ¯ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 2 \bar{\delta}_{\mathsf{ann}}^{2} appears in the time-averaged convergence bound. Since { α n } n = 0 M ​ N − 1 \{\alpha_{n}\}_{n=0}^{MN-1} is non-increasing, the proximal drifts are uniformly Λ η , 𝖺𝗇𝗇 \Lambda_{\eta,\mathsf{ann}} -Lipschitz, where Λ η , 𝖺𝗇𝗇 ≜ α 0 ​ L S + β L ​ 1 + η ​ α 0 ​ L S 1 − η ​ α L , q 𝖺𝗇𝗇 ≜ τ ​ Λ η , 𝖺𝗇𝗇 . \Lambda_{\eta,\mathsf{ann}}\,\triangleq\,\alpha_{0}L_{\mathsfit{S}}+\beta_{L}\frac{1+\eta\alpha_{0}L_{\mathsfit{S}}}{1-\eta\alpha_{L}},\quad q_{\mathsf{ann}}\,\triangleq\,\tau\Lambda_{\eta,\mathsf{ann}}. (45) Here, q 𝖺𝗇𝗇 q_{\mathsf{ann}} is the uniform in-block Picard contraction factor for multi-block APiX-MC. The following theorem states the convergence result for multi-block APiX-MC. Theorem 3 . Let ( μ t ) t ≥ 0 (\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0} denote the law of the continuous interpolation of { 𝒙 n ( K ) } n = 0 M ​ N \{{{\bm{x}}_{n}}^{(K)}\}_{n=0}^{MN} generated by multi-block APiX-MC, where N > 0 N>0 denotes the number of time steps in each time block and M > 0 M>0 is the number of blocks. Assume Assumptions 1 , 3 , and 4 hold, and choose sufficiently small parameters η , γ > 0 \eta,\gamma>0 . Then, the following inequality holds for multi-block APiX-MC: ( 0.75 − 𝒪 ( η 2 ) − 𝒪 ( γ 2 ) ) 1 T ∫ 0 T 𝖥𝖨 ( μ t ∥ π ) d t ≤ 𝖪𝖫 ( μ 0 ∥ π ) T + 𝒪 ⁡ ( η 2 ) ⏟ Splitting discrepancy + 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ ¯ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 2 ) ⏟ Annealed score mismatch error + 𝒪 ⁡ ( γ ) ⏟ Discretization error + 𝒪 ⁡ ( q 𝖺𝗇𝗇 2 ​ K − 2 ) ​ R 𝖺𝗇𝗇 ⏟ Finite Picard refinement error . \begin{array}[]{rl}&\Big(0.75-\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})-\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{2})\Big)\;\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathsf{FI}(\mu_{t}\|\pi)dt\\ \leq&\displaystyle\frac{\mathsf{KL}(\mu_{0}\|\pi)}{T}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Splitting}\\ \text{discrepancy}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(\bar{\delta}_{\mathsf{ann}}^{2})}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Annealed score }\\ \text{mismatch error}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(\gamma)}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Discretization}\\ \text{error}\end{subarray}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(q_{\mathsf{ann}}^{2K-2})\,R_{\mathsf{ann}}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{Finite Picard}\\ \text{refinement error}\end{subarray}}.\end{array} (46) where R 𝖺𝗇𝗇 = 2 ​ τ ​ d + 3 ​ τ 2 ​ ( δ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 2 + G 2 ) 1 − 3 ​ η 2 ​ β L 2 R_{\mathsf{ann}}=2\tau d+\frac{3\tau^{2}\left(\delta_{\mathsf{ann}}^{2}+G^{2}\right)}{1-3\eta^{2}\beta_{L}^{2}} . Proof. See Appendix E for the detailed proof and full expression of the terms. ∎ Theorem 3 extends the multi-block guarantee in Theorem 2 to the weighted annealing setting. Compared with multi-block PiX-MC, the score-mismatch term is replaced by the time-averaged annealed-score discrepancy δ ¯ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 2 \bar{\delta}_{\mathsf{ann}}^{2} , while the finite Picard-refinement error is governed by the uniform contraction factor q 𝖺𝗇𝗇 q_{\mathsf{ann}} . In particular, δ ¯ 𝖺𝗇𝗇 2 ≤ 2 M ​ N ​ ∑ n = 0 M ​ N − 1 δ n 2 + 2 ​ R S 2 M ​ N ​ ∑ n = 0 M ​ N − 1 ( α n − 1 ) 2 . \bar{\delta}_{\mathsf{ann}}^{2}\leq\frac{2}{MN}\sum\limits_{n=0}^{MN-1}\delta_{n}^{2}+\frac{2R_{\mathsfit{S}}^{2}}{MN}\sum\limits_{n=0}^{MN-1}(\alpha_{n}-1)^{2}. (47) The first term represents the approximation error of score networks, whereas the second term is induced by the score weights. If α n = 1 \alpha_{n}=1 after a finite annealing stage, which is true in our experiments, the latter contribution decreases as M ​ N MN increases. Meanwhile, with q 𝖺𝗇𝗇 < 1 q_{\mathsf{ann}}<1 , the finite Picard-refinement error decays geometrically with K K . More broadly, annealing and Picard refinement act on complementary aspects of the computation: annealing improves the sequential trajectory itself, reducing the effective sequential effort required to attain a given reconstruction quality, whereas Picard refinement reduces the wall-clock cost of evaluating that trajectory through time parallelism. Their gains can therefore compound in practice. As demonstrated in § 5 , APiX-MC yields additional wall-clock acceleration beyond trajectory parallelization.

sections.heading: 4 Numerical Validation of the Theory
sections.text: We consider a compressed sensing problem whose target posterior is available in closed form. This setting allows us to directly compare the empirical distributions generated by PiX-MC algorithms with the true posterior, providing direct empirical support for the convergence results established in our theorems. As the single-block implementation of PiX-MC is computationally demanding, we implement all variants of PiX-MC using their multi-block schemes, namely Algorithms 2 – 3 . For brevity, we omit the qualifier "multi-block" hereafter. All PiX-MC algorithms use eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup.
sections.text: We construct a Gaussian image prior p ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒙 , μ prior , Σ prior ) , p({\bm{x}})=\mathcal{N}\bigl({\bm{x}};\mu_{\textsf{prior}},\Sigma_{\textsf{prior}}\bigr), (48) where μ prior \mu_{\textsf{prior}} and Σ prior \Sigma_{\textsf{prior}} are estimated from 70,000 FFHQ images ( Karras et al., 2019 ) , after converting the images to grayscale and resizing them to 32 × 32 32\times 32 . sections.heading: Distribution-Level Results
sections.text: Figure 2 reports the empirical posterior mean and pixelwise standard deviation at the final time step, together with the evolution of 𝖬𝖬𝖣 2 \mathsf{MMD}^{2} over the sampling trajectory. All three PiX-MC instantiations accurately recover the posterior mean and uncertainty maps. As expected, PiX-MC with the analytical score most closely matches the true posterior, owing to the absence of score approximation error. The 𝖬𝖬𝖣 2 \mathsf{MMD}^{2} curves show that the empirical distributions produced by all three methods move toward the target posterior, providing empirical support for the finite-horizon stationarity bounds established in Theorems 2 – 3 . At the final time step, PiX-MC with the analytical score achieves the lowest 𝖬𝖬𝖣 2 \mathsf{MMD}^{2} of 0.0036 0.0036 , while APiX-MC and PiX-MC with the learned score attain 0.1361 0.1361 and 0.1480 0.1480 , respectively. The remaining gap between the learned-score variants and the analytical variant is consistent with the score approximation error analyzed in Section 3 . Compared with PiX-MC, APiX-MC reduces 𝖬𝖬𝖣 2 \mathsf{MMD}^{2} more rapidly and reaches a lower final value, corroborating the discussion in Section 3.4 that annealing improves the underlying sampling trajectory while Picard refinement enables its parallel evaluation.

sections.heading: 5 Real-World Imaging Experiments
sections.text: We now present our experimental results, which are organized around three goals. First, we verify the behavior of Picard refinement on MRI and Rician noise removal, covering both linear and nonlinear inverse problem setups. Second, we evaluate practical acceleration on large-scale 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 image deblurring, where we vary the GPU budget and the block size to examine how the multi-block implementation affects wall-clock runtime. Third, we apply PiX-MC to a large-scale 512 × 512 × 80 512\times 512\times 80 sparse-view CT problem to demonstrate its scalability on high-dimensional imaging tasks. All hyper-parameters are tuned to maximize the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) . Additional implementation details and hyper-parameter settings are provided in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Experimental Setup.
sections.text: All experiments are conducted on a single compute node equipped with eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs and two AMD EPYC 9334 32-Core processors. All Picard-based methods are implemented using the multi-block scheme and executed on all eight GPUs, whereas sequential methods are executed on a single GPU. We use DPS ( Chung et al., 2022 ) and DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) as external baselines. For the deblurring and 3D CT experiments, we additionally include sequential and ablation variants to isolate the effects of Picard time parallelization, the proximal-likelihood drift, and the annealing strategy. We use the following nomenclature throughout this section. L-MC denotes the standard sequential Langevin sampler with score network S θ {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta} (Eq. ( 9 )), and X-MC denotes its proximal-likelihood counterpart (Eq. ( 21 )). PiL-MC is obtained by applying Picard time parallelization to L-MC by replacing the drift T η \mathsfit{T}_{\eta} in Algorithm 2 with S θ + ∇ L {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}+\nabla L . The prefix “A” denotes the corresponding annealed variants, yielding AL-MC, AX-MC, and APiL-MC. Unless otherwise specified, all methods use the same score network for each imaging task. Task-specific score network choices and multi-block configurations are described in the corresponding subsections, while complete hyperparameter settings are provided in Appendix F.1 .

sections.heading: 5.1 Behavior of Picard Refinement
sections.text: We first present results on linear MRI reconstruction and nonlinear Rician denoising. These experiments empirically verify the geometric decay of the Picard error predicted by Lemmas 2 and 3 , demonstrating that the predicted convergence behavior is agnostic to the linearity of the inverse problem. Figure 3 : Visualization of the in-block Picard error ε m , k \varepsilon_{m,k} for PiX-MC methods on accelerated MRI reconstruction and Rician denoising. Langevin-based methods are included for reference. The error is plotted against the Picard iteration k k for representative blocks, using the block indexed by m = 5 m=5 for MRI reconstruction and the block indexed by m = 3 m=3 for Rician denoising. After a short initial transient, all PiX-MC methods exhibit geometric decay, consistent with Lemma 3 .

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: For MRI, we use the pretrained score network provided by ( Sun et al., 2024 ) 1 1 1 The pretrained score network is available at https://github.com/sunyumark/PnP-MonteCarlo . We use ten brain images with size 320 × 320 320\times 320 from the FastMRI dataset ( Zbontar et al., 2018 ) as the test set. We use a radial subsampling mask corresponding to 8 × 8\times acceleration. We additionally add additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) with standard deviation σ 𝒚 = 0.05 \sigma_{{\bm{y}}}=0.05 . For Rician denoising, we use the pretrained 256 × 256 256\times 256 unconditioned diffusion model 2 2 2 The pretrained diffusion model is available at https://github.com/openai/guided-diffusion . The tested dataset (CBSD10) is composed of a subset of 10 images of the CBSD68 dataset ( Martin et al., 2001 ) . We add Rician noise with σ 𝒚 = 0.1 \sigma_{{\bm{y}}}=0.1 . We set M = 10 , N = 75 , K = 100 M=10,N=75,K=100 for MRI, and M = 5 , N = 100 , K = 50 M=5,N=100,K=50 for Rician denoising. We refer to Appendix F.2 for more technical details on these two tasks.

sections.heading: Trajectory Evolution.
sections.text: We further visualize the evolution of the trajectories during the Picard iteration. Given an image 𝒙 {\bm{x}} and the ground-truth image 𝒙 𝖦𝖳 {\bm{x}}_{\mathsf{GT}} , we compute the mean-squared error (MSE) MSE := 1 d ​ ‖ 𝒙 − 𝒙 𝖦𝖳 ‖ 2 2 \text{MSE}:=\frac{1}{d}\left\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{x}}_{\mathsf{GT}}\right\|_{2}^{2} , and Figure 4 visualizes the resulting MSE curves. At the initial Picard iteration ( k = 0 k=0 ), all time nodes within each block are initialized to the same point, yielding piecewise-constant MSE curves. As the Picard iteration proceeds, the trajectories are progressively refined, and the piecewise-constant curves evolve into smooth trajectories across successive blocks. This evolution provides an intuitive illustration of the Picard refinement mechanism and is consistent with the convergence guarantees established in Lemma 3 and Theorems 2 – 3 . sections.heading: Quantitative and Qualitative Comparison.
sections.text: Now we evaluate the final reconstruction quality of the proposed methods. Table 1 reports the average quantitative results over ten test images for each task. For Rician denoising, APiL-MC achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM, while APiX-MC attains the lowest LPIPS. For accelerated MRI, APiX-MC achieves the best PSNR and SSIM among all compared methods. Overall, the proposed methods are competitive with diffusion-based baselines, and annealing consistently improves reconstruction quality over the corresponding non-annealed variants. Figures 5 – 6 provide visual comparisons. For accelerated MRI, TV exhibits staircase artifacts, while DAPS leaves noticeable residual noise. Both PiL-MC and APiL-MC remove most blur and noise but lose fine image details. In contrast, PiX-MC and APiX-MC recover sharper edges with fewer residual artifacts, as highlighted in the zoomed-in regions of Figure 5 . A similar trend is observed for Rician denoising. DPS exhibits noticeable color shifts, and DAPS leaves residual noise in the regions highlighted in purple. While PiL-MC and APiL-MC effectively suppress the Rician noise, PiX-MC and APiX-MC preserve finer structures. In particular, APiX-MC successfully reconstructs the letter “A” together with the surrounding dot-like markings (red box), whereas these details are blurred into a thin horizontal line by PiX-MC and are absent from the remaining reconstructions. These visual observations are consistent with the quantitative results in Table 1 .

sections.heading: 5.2 Practical Acceleration on Large-Scale Deblurring
sections.text: In this section, we investigate whether Picard time parallelization can accelerate posterior sampling without sacrificing reconstruction quality, and how this acceleration scales with the GPU budget and the number of time nodes per block.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: For the score network, we use the same diffusion model as in the Rician noise removal experiment. We use ten natural images from the DIV2K validation set from ( Agustsson and Timofte, 2017 ) 3 3 3 The DIV2K dataset is available at https://data.vision.ee.ethz.ch/cvl/DIV2K/ . We center-crop each image to size 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 . We apply a camera-shake blur from ( Levin et al., 2009 ) to the test images, and add AWGN noise with standard deviation σ 𝒚 = 0.05 \sigma_{{\bm{y}}}=0.05 . For the proximal methods, the proximal operator on likelihood can be solved efficiently in the Fourier domain according to ( Pan et al., 2016 ) . For each block of the Picard-based methods, we adopt an adaptive stopping criterion: the Picard refinement is terminated when either the maximum number of Picard iterations K = 20 K=20 is reached, or the normalized Picard error satisfies ε m , k / d < 3 × 10 − 4 \varepsilon_{m,k}/d<3\times 10^{-4} . More implementation details are provided in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Acceleration under Different Parallelization Configurations.
sections.text: We first investigate the practical acceleration under different numbers of GPUs and time nodes N N within each block. Table 2 reports the runtime for reaching an average PSNR of 26 26 dB and the corresponding speedup over each sequential counterpart under different configurations. It can be seen that increasing the number of GPUs improves the speedup across all tested methods and block configurations. In particular, using eight GPUs with N = 8 N=8 yields speedups between 2.87 × 2.87\times and 2.99 × 2.99\times across the four Picard-based methods, as all eight time nodes can be evaluated concurrently. Moderate oversubscription with N = 16 N=16 remains effective, but the benefit decreases as N N increasingly exceeds the number of available GPUs. For example, with four GPUs and N = 32 N=32 , all four Picard-based methods are slower than their sequential counterparts. These results demonstrate the practical trade-off between the block length and the available computational resources. Figure 7 : Average PSNR against wall-clock time for large-scale deblurring. The left and right panels show the non-annealed and annealed methods, respectively. The horizontal dashed line marks the reference PSNR of 26 26 dB, and the vertical dotted lines indicate the corresponding threshold-crossing time in seconds. Note how PiX-MC and APiX-MC substantially accelerate convergence without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Figure 7 plots the average PSNR against runtime in seconds under the configuration of eight GPUs and N = 8 N=8 . As shown, Picard parallelization consistently accelerates convergence. In particular, APiX-MC reaches an average PSNR of 26 26 dB in only 54 54 seconds, compared with 157 157 seconds for AX-MC, 365 365 seconds for X-MC, and 491 491 seconds for L-MC. Beyond the pairwise speedups, this comparison demonstrates that Picard time parallelization can compound with mechanisms that accelerate the underlying sequential trajectory. For example, the proximal update and annealing together reduce the runtime from 491 491 seconds for L-MC to 157 157 seconds for AX-MC, corresponding to a 3.13 × 3.13\times sequential-side speedup. Picard parallelization further reduces this runtime to 54 54 seconds, providing an additional 2.91 × 2.91\times parallelization-side speedup. Together, they yield an overall 9 × 9\times speedup over L-MC. These results empirically support the discussion at the end of § 3.4 that Picard parallelization provides a complementary direction that can be combined with sequential strategies. This is particularly valuable for large-scale imaging tasks, where sequential trajectory evaluation is computationally expensive.

sections.heading: 5.3 Scaling to 3D CT Reconstruction
sections.text: Finally, we evaluate PiX-MC on a large-scale sparse-view CT reconstruction problem with volume size 512 × 512 × 80 512\times 512\times 80 , demonstrating its practical scalability to high-dimensional 3D imaging.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: For the score network, we trained a diffusion model based on the EDM framework ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , using CT images from the AMOS ( Ji et al., 2022 ) and LDCT ( Moen et al., 2021 ) datasets. The image values in Hounsfield units were clamped to the range [ − 1000 , 1000 ] [-1000,1000] , then linearly rescaled to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . We consider a sparse-view parallel-beam CT reconstruction problem with 30 uniformly spaced projection views over 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} . The target volume consists of 80 axial slices, each of size 512 × 512 512\times 512 . Measurements are generated by applying the parallel-beam projection operator and adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ 𝒚 = 0.5 \sigma_{{\bm{y}}}=0.5 in the sinogram domain. Filtered back-projection (FBP) is used for initialization. Forward projection, back projection, and FBP are implemented using LEAP ( Kim and Champley, ) 4 4 4 LEAP is available at https://github.com/LLNL/LEAP . To encourage consistency across adjacent slices, we additionally incorporate a one-dimensional inter-slice Huber-TV (HTV) regularizer 𝑯 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) {\bm{H}}({\bm{x}}) into the proximal drift. The detailed formulation of the HTV regularizer and the resulting proximal drift are provided in Appendix F.2 . Accordingly, the proximal drift T η , σ \mathsfit{T}_{\eta,\sigma} is given by T η , σ ≜ 1 η ( I − 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 η ​ L ∘ ( I − η S θ ( ⋅ ; σ ) − η β H ∇ 𝑯 ) ) , \mathsfit{T}_{\eta,\sigma}\,\triangleq\,\frac{1}{\eta}\Big(I-\mathsf{prox}_{\eta L}\circ\big(I-\eta{\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}(\cdot;\sigma)-\eta\beta_{H}\nabla{\bm{H}}\big)\Big), (52) where β H > 0 \beta_{H}>0 is a balancing parameter for 𝑯 {\bm{H}} . All Picard-based methods use eight GPUs with N = 8 N=8 time nodes per block. Figure 10 : Visual comparison of PiX-MC and baseline methods for large-scale sparse-view 3D CT reconstruction. The 20th slice of a 512 × 512 × 80 512\times 512\times 80 CT volume is shown. Green boxes indicate the zoomed-in regions, together with the corresponding residual maps. The PSNR values and runtime (minutes) after convergence are reported. Note how APiX-MC achieves the best visual quality and the highest PSNR of 33.64 33.64 dB in only 35 35 minutes, by combining Picard iteration, annealing, and the proximal-likelihood drift.

sections.heading: Runtime Acceleration.
sections.text: Figure 9 plots the mean slice-wise PSNR over the 80 axial slices against wall-clock time. The curves distinguish the effects of the three algorithmic components: the proximal-likelihood drift, Picard time parallelization, and annealing. Compared with their likelihood-gradient counterparts, X-MC and AX-MC converge substantially faster and attain higher final PSNR, demonstrating that the proximal-likelihood drift provides a more effective reconstruction trajectory for this CT task. Building upon these improved trajectories, PiX-MC and APiX-MC further reduce the wall-clock time while preserving the attainable reconstruction quality. Specifically, PiX-MC reaches its reference PSNR in only 37 37 minutes, compared with 116 116 minutes for X-MC, corresponding to a 3.14 × 3.14\times speedup. Likewise, APiX-MC requires only 9 9 minutes, compared with 28 28 minutes for AX-MC, yielding a 3.11 × 3.11\times speedup. The same pattern is observed for the likelihood-gradient methods, where PiL-MC and APiL-MC accelerate L-MC and AL-MC by 3.08 × 3.08\times and 2.96 × 2.96\times , respectively. Annealing further improves the attainable reconstruction quality while preserving the approximately 3 × 3\times speedup provided by Picard time parallelization. Overall, APiX-MC achieves 32.5 dB in only 9 9 minutes, demonstrating how the proximal-likelihood drift, annealing, and Picard time parallelization compound to deliver approximately a 50 × 50\times wall-clock speedup over the standard L-MC.

sections.heading: Axial-Slice and Volumetric Reconstruction.
sections.text: Figures 10 and 11 compare the reconstructed axial slice after convergence and the reconstructed volume under a fixed wall-clock budget of 35 35 minutes, respectively. Across all four sequential/Picard pairs, Picard time parallelization achieves comparable or better reconstruction quality in substantially less wall-clock time. The visual comparisons further separate the effects of the remaining algorithmic components: compared with the likelihood-gradient methods, the proximal-likelihood variants more effectively suppress sparse-view streak artifacts and recover finer anatomical structures, while annealing further reduces residual artifacts and improves visual fidelity. These improvements are consistently observed in both the selected axial slice and the full 3D volume. Overall, APiX-MC achieves the best visual quality, and the two figures together demonstrate that the proximal-likelihood drift, annealing, and Picard time parallelization complement each other to enable high-quality large-scale 3D CT reconstruction. Figure 11 : Visual comparison of PiX-MC and baseline methods for large-scale sparse-view 3D CT reconstruction under a 35-minute time budget. Note how APiX-MC substantially suppresses the streak artifacts and noise while preserving clear structures.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper introduces PiX-MC, a principled time-parallel posterior sampling framework for Bayesian imaging. Motivated by forward-backward splitting, we construct a proximal drift that exploits efficient proximal operators available for imaging likelihoods. Instead of advancing the samples sequentially along a long trajectory, PiX-MC parallelizes the trajectory across time nodes, enabling multiple time nodes to be processed concurrently across GPUs. To improve practical scalability under limited GPU budgets, we further develop annealed and multi-block variants. The annealed variant empirically accelerates the convergence to reach a target reconstruction quality, while the multi-block variant partitions the trajectory into blocks, allowing PiX-MC to operate efficiently under limited GPU budgets. We establish finite-time stationarity guarantees for all variants of PiX-MC under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments across linear, nonlinear, and large-scale 2D and 3D imaging problems demonstrate practical scalability of PiX-MC and substantial wall-clock acceleration while maintaining reconstruction quality.

sections.heading: F.1 Common Implementation Details and Hyperparameter Selections
sections.text: In all experiments, the images are scaled to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Before evaluating a score network, we rescale the input image to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] and map the network output back to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] accordingly. The pretrained models used for natural images, MRI, and CT adopt different output parameterizations, whose model-specific implementations are described below.

sections.heading: Score-network implementation.
sections.text: For the natural-image experiments, we employ a pretrained diffusion model as in DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) . Let α ¯ t \bar{\alpha}_{t} denote the cumulative diffusion coefficient. The connection between the score network S θ {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta} and noise predictor ε θ \varepsilon_{\theta} in DDPM can be formulated approximately as S θ ​ ( 𝒙 , σ ) = 2 σ ​ ε θ ​ ( 2 ​ 𝒙 − 𝟏 1 + σ 2 , σ ) , {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}};\sigma)=\displaystyle\frac{2}{\sigma}\varepsilon_{\theta}\left(\frac{2{\bm{x}}-\bm{1}}{\sqrt{1+\sigma^{2}}};\sigma\right), (200) where σ = 1 − α ¯ t α ¯ t \sigma=\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}} . For MRI reconstruction, we employ the pretrained score network from PMC ( Sun et al., 2024 ) . Denote its output in the network coordinates by S θ 𝖬𝖱𝖨 ​ ( 2 ​ 𝒙 − 𝟏 , σ ) {\mathsfit{S}}^{\mathsf{MRI}}_{\theta}(2{\bm{x}}-\bm{1};\sigma) . Since the network directly estimates the positive score, the negative-score function used in our formulation is S θ ​ ( 𝒙 , σ ) = − 2 ​ S θ 𝖬𝖱𝖨 ​ ( 2 ​ 𝒙 − 𝟏 , σ ) . {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}};\sigma)=-2{\mathsfit{S}}^{\mathsf{MRI}}_{\theta}(2{\bm{x}}-\bm{1};\sigma). (201) For CT images, we train an MMSE denoiser D θ {\mathsfit{D}}_{\theta} using the standard EDM framework ( Karras et al., 2022 ) . The relation between S θ {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta} and D θ {\mathsfit{D}}_{\theta} is S θ ​ ( 𝒙 , σ ) = 2 σ 2 ​ [ 2 ​ 𝒙 − 𝟏 − D θ ​ ( 2 ​ 𝒙 − 𝟏 , σ ) ] . {\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}};\sigma)=\displaystyle\frac{2}{\sigma^{2}}\left[2{\bm{x}}-\bm{1}-{\mathsfit{D}}_{\theta}(2{\bm{x}}-\bm{1};\sigma)\right]. (202)

sections.heading: Balancing parameter for likelihood.
sections.text: To account for the different numerical scales of the likelihood and score networks, we introduce a task-dependent balancing parameter λ > 0 \lambda>0 for the likelihood. For example, MRI, deblurring, and CT, the likelihood is L ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = λ 2 ​ ‖ 𝑨 ​ 𝒙 − 𝒚 ‖ 2 , L({\bm{x}})=\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{2}\|{\bm{A}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|^{2}, (203) where 𝑨 {\bm{A}} is a task-specific forward operator.

sections.heading: Annealing Schedule.
sections.text: Let n = m ​ N + i n=mN+i denote the global time node index, where m = 0 , … , M − 1 m=0,\ldots,M-1 is the block index and i = 0 , … , N − 1 i=0,\ldots,N-1 is the local node index. Recall that we use the geometric schedule σ n = 𝗆𝖺𝗑 { σ 𝗆𝖺𝗑 ​ ξ n , σ 𝗆𝗂𝗇 } , \sigma_{n}=\mathop{\mathsf{max}}\{\sigma_{\mathop{\mathsf{max}}}\xi^{n},\sigma_{\mathop{\mathsf{min}}}\}, (204) where 0 < ξ < 1 0<\xi<1 is the annealing parameter. For the score network weight schedule α n \alpha_{n} , we also use a corresponding geometric sequence α n = ( σ n / σ 𝗆𝗂𝗇 ) a \alpha_{n}=(\sigma_{n}/\sigma_{\mathop{\mathsf{min}}})^{a} (205) This schedule is non-increasing and becomes one once σ n \sigma_{n} reaches σ 𝗆𝗂𝗇 \sigma_{\mathop{\mathsf{min}}} . For the MRI and CT experiments, we set a = 2 a=2 ; for the deblurring and Rician denoising experiments, we set a = 5 / 2 a=5/2 .

sections.heading: Picard stopping criteria.
sections.text: For deblurring and CT experiments, we employ adaptive Picard refinement. We compute the empirical in-block residual ε m , k = 𝗆𝖺𝗑 1 ≤ i ≤ N ‖ 𝒙 m ​ N + i ( k ) − 𝒙 m ​ N + i ( k − 1 ) ‖ . \varepsilon_{m,k}=\mathop{\mathsf{max}}\limits_{1\leq i\leq N}\left\|{\bm{x}}_{mN+i}^{(k)}-{\bm{x}}_{mN+i}^{(k-1)}\right\|. (206) The refinement within a block is terminated when either k k reaches K = 20 K=20 or the normalized residual ε m , k / d < 3 × 10 − 4 \varepsilon_{m,k}/d<3\times 10^{-4} .

sections.heading: Hyperparameter selection.
sections.text: The hyperparameters are tuned separately for each method and imaging task to obtain the best reconstruction results. The gradient-based and proximal variants use different drift parameterizations and are therefore assigned method-specific stepsizes. In particular, the implicit treatment of the likelihood in the proximal variants may improve numerical stability and permit larger stepsizes in practice. For each paired sequential and Picard-based method, we use the same Langevin stepsize, score schedule, likelihood weight, and total number of time nodes. sections.heading: F.2 Likelihood and Proximal Implementations
sections.text: We next provide the task-specific implementations of the likelihood gradient and proximal operator. The datasets, score networks, and hyperparameters are reported in $ 5 and Appendix F.1 .

sections.heading: MRI reconstruction.
sections.text: The forward operator 𝑨 = 𝑴 ​ ℱ {\bm{A}}={\bm{M}}\mathcal{F} consists of the discrete Fourier transform ℱ \mathcal{F} followed by a radial subsampling mask. The likelihood and its gradient are L ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = λ 2 ​ ‖ 𝑴 ​ ℱ ​ 𝒙 − 𝒚 ‖ 2 , ∇ L ​ ( 𝒙 ) = λ ​ ℱ H ​ 𝑴 T ​ ( 𝑴 ​ ℱ ​ 𝒙 − 𝒚 ) . L({\bm{x}})=\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{2}\|{\bm{M}}\mathcal{F}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|^{2},\quad\nabla L({\bm{x}})=\lambda\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{H}}{\bm{M}}^{\mathrm{T}}\left({\bm{M}}\mathcal{F}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\right). (207) The proximal operator has the closed form 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 η ​ L ​ ( 𝒛 ) = ( η ​ λ ​ ℱ H ​ 𝑴 T ​ 𝑴 ​ ℱ + I ) − 1 ​ ( 𝒛 + η ​ λ ​ ℱ H ​ 𝑴 T ​ 𝒚 ) . \mathsf{prox}_{\eta L}({\bm{z}})=\left(\eta\lambda\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{H}}{\bm{M}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{M}}\mathcal{F}+I\right)^{-1}\left({\bm{z}}+\eta\lambda\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{H}}{\bm{M}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{y}}\right). (208) Since ℱ \mathcal{F} is unitary and 𝑴 T ​ 𝑴 {\bm{M}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{M}} is diagonal in the Fourier domain, the inverse above can be evaluated elementwise in k-space, without the need to solve a large-scale linear system.

sections.heading: Rician denoising.
sections.text: Let 𝒆 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝗅 {\bm{e}}_{\mathsf{real}} and 𝒆 𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗀 {\bm{e}}_{\mathsf{imag}} be two i.i.d. Gaussian noise vectors with zero mean and standard deviation σ 𝒚 \sigma_{{\bm{y}}} . The Rician-noise-corrupted observation 𝒚 {\bm{y}} is obtained by: 𝒚 = ( 𝒙 + 𝒆 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝗅 ) 2 + 𝒆 𝗂𝗆𝖺𝗀 2 , {\bm{y}}=\sqrt{({\bm{x}}+{\bm{e}}_{\mathsf{real}})^{2}+{\bm{e}}_{\mathsf{imag}}^{2}}, (209) where theoperations are elementwise. According to ( Gudbjartsson and Patz, 1995 ) , the conditional probability density function (PDF) of 𝒚 {\bm{y}} is p ⁡ ( 𝒚 | 𝒙 ) = ∏ r = 1 d 𝒚 r σ 𝒚 2 ​ 𝖾𝗑𝗉 ​ ( − 𝒙 r 2 + 𝒚 r 2 2 ​ σ 𝒚 2 ) ​ I 0 ​ ( 𝒙 r ​ 𝒚 r σ 𝒚 2 ) , p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\prod_{r=1}^{d}\frac{{\bm{y}}_{r}}{\sigma_{{\bm{y}}}^{2}}\mathsf{exp}\left(-\frac{{\bm{x}}_{r}^{2}+{\bm{y}}_{r}^{2}}{2\sigma_{{\bm{y}}}^{2}}\right)I_{0}\left(\frac{{\bm{x}}_{r}{\bm{y}}_{r}}{\sigma_{{\bm{y}}}^{2}}\right), (210) which is known as the Rice or Rician distribution. Here I 0 I_{0} is the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order zero. Consider the modified Bessel’s differential equations: x 2 ​ y ′′ + x ​ y ′ − ( x 2 + n 2 ) ​ y = 0 , n ≥ 0 . \displaystyle x^{2}y^{\prime\prime}+xy^{\prime}-(x^{2}+n^{2})y=0,\quad n\geq 0. The solutions of the previous equation I n ​ ( x ) = y ​ ( x ) I_{n}(x)=y(x) continuous in zero are called the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order n n . After omitting terms independent of 𝒙 {\bm{x}} , the negative log-likelihood L L for Rician noise removal is L ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = λ ⁡ ⟨ 𝟏 , 𝒙 2 2 ​ σ 𝒚 2 − 𝗅𝗈𝗀 ​ I 0 ​ ( 𝒙 ⊙ 𝒚 σ 𝒚 2 ) ⟩ . L({\bm{x}})=\lambda\displaystyle\left\langle\bm{1},\frac{{\bm{x}}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}_{{\bm{y}}}}-\mathsf{log\,}I_{0}\left(\frac{{\bm{x}}\odot{\bm{y}}}{\sigma^{2}_{{\bm{y}}}}\right)\right\rangle. (211) Note that according to Lemma 12 in ( Renaud et al., 2026b ) , L L is Lipschitz smooth, thus satisfies Assumption 1 . Following ( Wei et al., 2023 ) , its gradient is evaluated using the ratio B ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = I 1 ​ ( 𝒙 ) / I 0 ​ ( 𝒙 ) B({\bm{x}})=I_{1}({\bm{x}})/I_{0}({\bm{x}}) , and the pixel-wise proximal subproblem is solved using the iterative reweighted ℓ 1 \ell_{1} (IRL1) method. The IRL1 algorithm for solving 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 η ​ L ​ ( 𝒛 ) \mathsf{prox}_{\eta L}(\bm{z}) is given as follows: 𝒙 t + 1 2 = 𝒚 σ y 2 ​ B ​ ( 𝒙 t ⊙ 𝒚 σ y 2 ) 𝒙 t + 1 = arg 𝗆𝗂𝗇 𝒙 η λ ⟨ 1 , 𝒙 2 2 ​ σ 𝒚 2 − 𝒙 ⊙ 𝒚 σ 𝒚 2 ⟩ + 1 2 ∥ 𝒙 − 𝒛 ∥ 2 − η λ ⟨ 𝒙 t + 1 2 , 𝒙 ⟩ = 𝒛 + η ​ λ σ 𝒚 2 ​ 𝒚 + η ​ λ ​ 𝒙 t + 1 2 1 + η ​ λ σ 𝒚 2 . \begin{array}[]{rl}\bm{x}^{t+\frac{1}{2}}&=\displaystyle\frac{\bm{y}}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}B\left(\frac{\bm{x}^{t}\bm{\odot y}}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}\right)\\ \bm{x}^{t+1}&=\displaystyle\arg\mathop{\mathsf{min}}\limits_{{\bm{x}}}\eta\lambda\left\langle\textbf{1},\frac{\bm{x}^{2}}{2\sigma_{{\bm{y}}}^{2}}-\frac{\bm{x\odot y}}{\sigma_{{\bm{y}}}^{2}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{x-z}\|^{2}-\eta\lambda\langle\bm{x}^{t+\frac{1}{2}},\bm{x}\rangle\\ &=\displaystyle\frac{\displaystyle\bm{z}+\frac{\eta\lambda}{\sigma_{{\bm{y}}}^{2}}\bm{y}+\eta\lambda\bm{x}^{t+\frac{1}{2}}}{1+\displaystyle\frac{\eta\lambda}{\sigma_{{\bm{y}}}^{2}}}.\end{array} (212) In experiments, we set the maximum inner iteration number for IRL1 to be 10 10 because it typically solves the proximal sub-problem within 5 5 iterations.

sections.heading: Image deblurring.
sections.text: Following ( Renaud et al., 2026b ) , we model the forward operator as a circular convolution, which is diagonalized by the discrete Fourier transform. The likelihood is L ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = λ 2 ​ ‖ 𝑲 ​ 𝒙 − 𝒚 ‖ 2 L({\bm{x}})=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|{\bm{K}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|^{2} , where 𝑲 {\bm{K}} is the circular convolution operator associated with a blur kernel 𝒌 {\bm{k}} . The likelihood gradient and proximal operator are ∇ L ​ ( 𝒙 ) = λ ​ 𝑲 T ​ ( 𝑲 ​ 𝒙 − 𝒚 ) , 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 η ​ L ​ ( 𝒛 ) = ( η ​ λ ​ 𝑲 T ​ 𝑲 + I ) − 1 ​ ( 𝒛 + η ​ λ ​ 𝑲 T ​ 𝒚 ) . \nabla L({\bm{x}})=\lambda{\bm{K}}^{\mathrm{T}}({\bm{K}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}),\quad\mathsf{prox}_{\eta L}({\bm{z}})=\left(\eta\lambda{\bm{K}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{K}}+I\right)^{-1}({\bm{z}}+\eta\lambda{\bm{K}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{y}}). (213) The proximal operator can be evaluated efficiently in the Fourier domain through elementwise multiplication and division: 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 η ​ L ​ ( 𝒛 ) = ℱ H ​ ( ℱ ⁡ ( 𝒛 + η ​ λ ​ 𝑲 T ​ 𝒚 ) ℱ ⁡ ( η ​ λ ​ 𝑲 T ​ 𝑲 + 𝟏 ) ) . \mathsf{prox}_{\eta L}({\bm{z}})=\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{H}}\left(\frac{\mathcal{F}({\bm{z}}+\eta\lambda{\bm{K}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{y}})}{\mathcal{F}(\eta\lambda{\bm{K}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{K}}+\bm{1})}\right). (214)

sections.heading: 3D CT reconstruction.
sections.text: The quadratic likelihood potential and its gradient are given by L ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = λ 2 ​ ‖ 𝑨 ​ 𝒙 − 𝒚 ‖ 2 , ∇ L ​ ( 𝒙 ) = λ ​ 𝑨 T ​ ( 𝑨 ​ 𝒙 − 𝒚 ) . L({\bm{x}})=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|{\bm{A}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|^{2},\quad\nabla L({\bm{x}})=\lambda{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{T}}({\bm{A}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}). (215) The proximal operator is evaluated by solving the following linear system: 𝒙 = 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 η ​ L ​ ( 𝒛 ) ⇔ ( I + η ​ λ ​ 𝑨 T ​ 𝑨 ) ​ 𝒙 = 𝒛 + η ​ λ ​ 𝑨 T ​ 𝒚 . {\bm{x}}=\mathsf{prox}_{\eta L}({\bm{z}})\iff(I+\eta\lambda{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{A}}){\bm{x}}={\bm{z}}+\eta\lambda{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{T}}{\bm{y}}. (216) We solve this linear system using five conjugate gradient iterations ( Shewchuk and others, 1994 ) . To promote consistency between adjacent slices, we additionally use a one-dimensional inter-slice Huber-TV (HTV) regularizer. For 𝒙 ∈ ℝ 512 × 512 × 80 {\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{512\times 512\times 80} , HTV regularizer 𝑯 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) {\bm{H}}({\bm{x}}) with smoothing parameter δ H > 0 \delta_{\textsf{H}}>0 is 𝑯 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) = ∑ i = 1 512 ∑ j = 1 512 ∑ s = 1 79 H δ H ​ ( 𝒙 ⁡ ( i , j , s + 1 ) − 𝒙 ⁡ ( i , j , s ) ) , {\bm{H}}({\bm{x}})=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{512}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{512}\sum\limits_{s=1}^{79}H_{\delta_{\textsf{H}}}({\bm{x}}(i,j,s+1)-{\bm{x}}(i,j,s)), (217) where 𝒙 ⁡ ( i , j , s ) {\bm{x}}(i,j,s) denotes the element located at i i -th row, j j -th column in s s -th slice. For any x ∈ ℝ x\in\mathbb{R} , H δ H ​ ( x ) H_{\delta_{\textsf{H}}}(x) is defined as H δ H ​ ( x ) := { x 2 2 ​ δ H , if ​ | x | ≤ δ H ; | x | − δ H 2 , if ​ | x | > δ H . H_{\delta_{\textsf{H}}}(x):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}&\displaystyle\frac{x^{2}}{2\delta_{\textsf{H}}},&\text{if }|x|\leq\delta_{\textsf{H}};\\ &|x|-\displaystyle\frac{\delta_{\textsf{H}}}{2},&\text{if }|x|>\delta_{\textsf{H}}.\end{array}\right. (218) We set δ H = 10 − 8 \delta_{\textsf{H}}=10^{-8} in the experiments. We view HTV as an inter-slice prior for CT volumes characterizing correlations between adjacent slices. Accordingly, the proximal drift T η , σ \mathsfit{T}_{\eta,\sigma} is T η , σ ≜ 1 η ( I − 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 η ​ L ∘ ( I − η S θ ( ⋅ ; σ ) − η β H ∇ 𝑯 ) ) , \mathsfit{T}_{\eta,\sigma}\,\triangleq\,\frac{1}{\eta}\Big(I-\mathsf{prox}_{\eta L}\circ\big(I-\eta{\mathsfit{S}}_{\theta}(\cdot;\sigma)-\eta\beta_{H}\nabla{\bm{H}}\big)\Big), (219) where β H > 0 \beta_{H}>0 is a balancing parameter for 𝑯 {\bm{H}} . We set β H = 0.28 \beta_{H}=0.28 for all methods.

Picard Proximal Monte Carlo for Parallel Bayesian Imaging with Score-Based Generative Priors Deliang Wei 1 Evan Bell 1 Wenhan Guo 1 Yifan Chen 2 and Yu Sun 1, ✉ Address: 1 Johns Hopkins University 2 University of California, Los Angeles ✉ Corresponding author: ysun214@jh.edu Abstract Bayesian imaging inverse problems often require sampling from high-dimensional posterior distributions. While recent score-based and diffusion models provide expressive Bayesian priors, their sampling procedures remain inherently sequential and computationally expensive for large-scale imaging applications. We propose PiX-MC , a time-parallel posterior sampling framework based on proximal Langevin dynamics and Picard iteration. The proximal-likelihood formulation exploits the fact that many imaging likelihoods admit efficient, problem-specific proximal operators, while Picard refinement exposes parallelism across discretization nodes and naturally supports multi-GPU implementation. To further improve practical scalability and sampling performance, we develop multi-block and annealed variants of the proposed framework. We establish convergence guarantees under transparent assumptions, accommodating non-log-concave posteriors, imperfect learned score models, multi-block implementations, and annealing schedules. Experiments on a diverse collection of imaging inverse problems demonstrate that PiX-MC substantially reduces wall-clock time while preserving reconstruction quality. On a 512 × 512 × 80 512	imes 512	imes 80 sparse-view computed tomography (CT) problem, annealed multi-block PiX-MC achieves up to a 50 × 50	imes runtime speedup over the standard Langevin sampler using eight GPUs. 1 Introduction The recovery of an unknown image 𝒙 ∈ ℝ d { m{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from a set of sparse and noisy measurements 𝒚 ∈ ℝ c { m{y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c} is a fundamental problem in computational imaging. It is often mathematically formulated as an inverse problem of the following system 𝒚 = 𝑨 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) + 𝒆 , { m{y}}={ m{A}}({ m{x}})+{ m{e}}, (1) where the forward operator 𝑨 : ℝ d → ℝ c { m{A}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}ightarrow\mathbb{R}^{c} models the imaging system response and 𝒆 ∈ ℝ c { m{e}}\in\mathbb{R}^{c} denotes measurement noise. Due to the sparsity and noisiness of 𝒚 { m{y}} , multiple plausible 𝒙 { m{x}} can explain the same set of measurements, leading to significant uncertainty in the recovered image. Bayesian sampling methods offer a principled framework for addressing this ambiguity. Rather than seeking a single point estimate, they aim to characterize the full posterior distribution π ⁡ ( 𝒙 | 𝒚 ) \pi({ m{x}}|{ m{y}}) given an image prior p ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) p({ m{x}}) . This capability is particularly beneficial in high-stakes biomedical and scientific imaging applications, where different imaging results can lead to different scientific conclusions, clinical decisions, or downstream actions ( Begoli et al., 2019 ; Kampourakis and McCain, 2019 ) . Traditionally, the image prior is handcrafted, including total variation and sparsity-promoting penalties ( Rudin et al., 1992 ; Sauer and Bouman, 1992 ; Gu et al., 2014 ) ; yet such priors often fall short in capturing the complexity of real-world image distributions. Recently, score-based diffusion models (SDMs) have emerged as a powerful class of generative models capable of modeling such complexity, inspiring a growing body of work on SDM-based posterior sampling for imaging inverse problems. One popular line of work incorporates measurements as guidance to steer the generative process toward the posterior distribution ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Chung et al., 2022 ) ; this approach is convenient to implement on top of pre-trained models and has been demonstrated across a wide range of imaging applications ( Chung and Ye, 2022 ; Song et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ) . However, such guidance-based methods generally lack theoretical guarantees on whether the generated samples indeed follow the true posterior, significantly limiting their interpretability and reliability in high-stakes settings. In light of this, another class of methods integrates SDMs with classical Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) frameworks, providing more rigorous posterior sampling guarantees ( Brooks et al., 2011 ) . Popular instantiations include combining Langevin dynamics with the score network of an SDM ( Jalal et al., 2021 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) , and incorporating a full SDM as an empirical proximal sampler in the split Gibbs process ( Coeurdoux et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Despite their algorithmic differences, these methods share a common sequential structure: samples must be evolved through long iterative trajectories, each requiring repeated evaluations of both the score model and the forward operator. As a result, the computational cost scales poorly with the problem dimension and the complexity of the forward model, making large-scale imaging applications particularly challenging. This limitation is increasingly pronounced as modern machine learning systems are routinely deployed on multiple graphics processing unit (multi-GPU) platforms that offer substantial Figure 1 : Schematic illustration of the proposed Picard Proximal Monte Carlo (PiX-MC) method. PiX-MC employs time-batch processing and exploits Picard iteration to enable parallel computation across time nodes. parallel computational resources; yet existing samplers are not designed to exploit such parallelism. While efforts have explored parallelism for solvers applicable to inverse problems ( Lian et al., 2015 ; Zhou et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2021 ) , they are largely restricted to deterministic optimization frameworks, limiting the direct applicability of these techniques to posterior sampling. In this work, we bridge this gap by proposing Pi card pro X imal M onte C arlo ( PiX-MC ) , a time-parallel posterior sampling framework for scalable Bayesian imaging. PiX-MC is built upon a forward-backward splitting of Langevin dynamics that decouples the prior and likelihood, enabling modular integration of a score-based generative prior and a likelihood update via proximal mapping . To overcome the sequential bottleneck, PiX-MC further leverages Picard iteration to parallelize the sampling trajectory across time steps. A schematic illustration is provided in Figure 1 . The key contributions of this work are as follows: • We formulate the sampling trajectory of PiX-MC as a fixed-point problem and solve it via Picard iteration. Rather than parallelizing across image pixels, PiX-MC introduces parallelism across time steps, enabling concurrent processing over multiple GPUs. Unlike existing Picard-based methods ( Shih et al., 2023 ; Anari et al., 2024 ) , PiX-MC incorporates a forward–backward formulation that imposes measurement consistency through a proximal update. This design is particularly attractive for computational imaging, as it naturally exploits the structure of many imaging forward operators. We further develop annealed and multi-block variants of PiX-MC. The former employs temperature annealing to accelerate the underlying sequential sampling trajectory, while the latter partitions the sampling trajectory into multiple blocks, allowing PiX-MC to still operate efficiently under limited GPU budgets. • We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the proposed suite of PiX-MC algorithms. Our analysis bounds the time-averaged relative Fisher information by an O ⁡ ( 1 / T ) O(1/T) transient term together with explicit approximation-error terms. The theory accommodates imperfect learned score networks and weakly convex imaging likelihoods, covering practical settings encountered in a wide range of imaging problems. Furthermore, our results provide a detailed error decomposition that explicitly characterizes the individual contributions of forward–backward splitting, Picard iterations, and time discretization, offering interpretable insight into the sources of sampling error. • We validate PiX-MC on a diverse set of computational imaging inverse problems, including both linear and nonlinear forward models. In addition, we consider large-scale problems ranging from 1024 × 1024 1024	imes 1024 image deblurring to 512 × 512 × 80 512	imes 512	imes 80 sparse-view computed tomography (CT), covering both 2D and 3D imaging settings. These experiments are conducted on multi-GPU platforms to reflect realistic deployment conditions. The results demonstrate that PiX-MC generalizes across these settings while substantially reducing wall-clock time without sacrificing reconstruction quality. On the large-scale 3D CT task, APiX-MC achieves up to a 50 × 50	imes runtime speedup over the standard Langevin sampler using eight GPUs. 2 Background and Related Works We begin by reviewing regularized image reconstruction from a Bayesian perspective. We then introduce SDMs and discuss posterior sampling methods for imaging inverse problems. Finally, we review related parallelization approaches for image reconstruction. 2.1 Bayesian Image Reconstruction Classical approaches to imaging inverse problems are formulated as regularized optimization problems, seeking a solution that simultaneously fits the measurements and conforms to prior knowledge about the image. Starting from a learned generative diffusion process, the reverse dynamics are guided toward measurement-consistent samples through likelihood-based corrections ( Chung et al., 2022 ) or approximations of the posterior score ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . This viewpoint underlies a broad class of diffusion posterior sampling and guided diffusion methods, which have demonstrated strong empirical performance across a wide range of imaging tasks ( Chung and Ye, 2022 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Kawar et al., 2022 ; Rout et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Compared with Langevin-based approaches, however, these methods typically rely on approximations of the time-dependent posterior score and therefore do not always admit a straightforward characterization in terms of a target invariant distribution. 2.4 Related Parallel Imaging Methods & Picard Iteration Most existing parallel methods consider a general optimization formulation applicable to the MAP problem in ( 2 ). They accelerate computation by exploiting parallelism within individual iterations, including stochastic gradient methods ( Recht et al., 2011 ; Lian et al., 2017 ) , block-coordinate updates ( Fercoq and Richtárik, 2015 ; Richtárik and Takáč, 2016 ) , and asynchronous procedures ( Peng et al., 2016 ; Sun et al., 2017 ; Hannah et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2021 ) . Some of these techniques have also been extended to sampling ( Salim et al., 2019 ; Salim and Richtarik, 2020 ; Ding et al., 2021 ) . However, they do not reduce the intrinsic sequential structure of iterative algorithms, which remains the fundamental computational bottleneck for large-scale posterior sampling. A more recent line of work seeks to parallelize the sampling trajectory itself. In image generation, Picard iteration has been used to evaluate multiple denoising steps simultaneously ( Shih et al., 2023 ; So et al., 2025 ) . PiX-MC significantly extends this line of work to posterior sampling for imaging inverse problems, and provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis that accommodates all these components. 3 Method: Picard Proximal Monte Carlo (PiX-MC) This section presents the proposed PiX-MC framework. We first construct a proximal-likelihood drift motivated by the FBS-style update, which induces a sequential proximal Langevin dynamics. We then reformulate the resulting dynamics using Picard iteration, enabling parallel computation across sequential time steps. We further establish finite-horizon bounds on the time-averaged relative Fisher information of PiX-MC under transparent assumptions. Finally, we introduce multi-block and annealed variants of PiX-MC to further improve scalability and imaging performance.
